title: Does Branding Affect Perceived Drug Safety?
authors: Hanu Tyagi (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Manuel Hermosilla (University of Illinois at Chicago); Andrew Ching (Johns Hopkins University)
abstract: We examine whether brand equity shapes perceptions of drug safety. Using FDA adverse event data, we find that after Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine success, reports of side effects for its drugs sizably fell, suggesting the firm’s enhanced brand favorably influenced public perceptions of its drug safety.

title: Misleading Science Maps: Firms’ Strategic Responses to Data Malpractice in Alzheimer’s Research
authors: Matteo Tranchero (The Wharton School); Christian Fons-Rosen (UC Merced); Lee Fleming (UC Berkeley)
abstract: Why do firms invest in basic science when they could rely on published academic research? We argue that one overlooked reason is the uncertain reliability of science itself. When basic science is required for product development, corporate control of the research process serves as a substitute for the low verifiability of findings produced externally. Firms retain in-house research capabilities to assess, produce, and validate the studies needed for their innovations, particularly in domains where science is less dependable. We investigate this argument in the context of Alzheimer’s preclinical research, where inappropriate image alterations provide an objective marker of unreliable data. Using a novel AI-based detection tool validated through manual review, we scan the entire field and document a rising trend of data issues in published science. Problematic cases are less frequent when firms lead academic-industry collaborations and are nearly absent in fully corporate-authored research. In domains where academic science is less reliable, firms are more likely to conduct basic research internally and to build their inventions on these in-house studies. Our results identify scientific reliability as a neglected determinant of the “research boundaries” of the firm.

title: Market Size, Biosimilar Entry, and Price Competition in U.S. Biologic Drug Markets
authors: Morgane Mouslim (University of Michigan ); Jeffrey  Mccullough (University of Michigan); Antonio Trujillo (Johns Hopkins University )
abstract:
Biologic drugs account for a rapidly growing share of U.S. pharmaceutical spending, yet competition from biosimilars has emerged unevenly and often later than anticipated. This study examines how market size, firm entry, and pricing dynamics interact in U.S. biologic drug markets. Using quarterly sales and net price data from 2010 to 2023, we analyze ten biologics with marketed biosimilars and two biologics whose exclusivity has expired without biosimilar entry. We apply an entry-threshold framework from industrial organization to estimate the minimum market size required to sustain successive biosimilar entrants and assess how competitive conduct evolves as markets mature. Entry thresholds are estimated using an ordered probit model, and pricing effects are evaluated using a difference-in-differences design with a Callaway and Sant'Anna approach to account for staggered biosimilar entry across molecules.

We find that larger markets support more biosimilar entrants and that the market size required to sustain additional entry declines with each competitor, consistent with increasing competitive pressure. The largest shift in competitive conduct occurs between the first and second entrants. Biosimilar entry is associated with substantial reductions in originator net prices, with average declines of approximately 78 percent following first entry.  . Entry threshold patterns suggest that while biologic markets do not exhibit perfect competition, they can become highly competitive with multiple biosimilar entrants.
Policies that lower barriers to early biosimilar entry may generate the most gains in competition and affordability. Interventions that accelerate initial entry, rather than those focused solely on increasing the total number of biosimilar competitors, may be most effective in reducing biologic drug spending.

title: Data Privacy Regulation and Innovation
authors: Sukhun Kang (UC Santa Barbara); Jennifer Kao (UCLA)
abstract: We investigate how data privacy regulations shape research and development. While such regulations aim to increase stakeholder privacy and data security, they can also introduce costs in settings where collecting, analyzing, and sharing sensitive data is central to innovation. We examine this tension in the context of the pharmaceutical industry and the European Union's (EU) General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the most comprehensive data privacy regulation to date. Leveraging firm-level variation in exposure to the GDPR, we find that the regulation lowers clinical trials by 18 percent. Firms also shift the types of projects they pursue: trials are less likely to include sites in the EU, be conducted across multiple countries, and target a narrower set of diseases. Research collaborations decline overall and shift away from new partners towards established relationships. When looking at project outcomes, we observe that trials take longer to complete, are less likely to succeed, and report results with greater delay. The decline in clinical trial activity is greatest among young firms. These findings reveal how data privacy regulations shape not only the rate of innovation, but also the process by which it is pursued and its outcomes.

title: Mind the Gap in Drug Development: Understanding the Whitespace Between Clinical Trials
authors: Sukhun Kang (UC Santa Barbara); Sandra Barbosu (New York University, Tandon School of Engineering); Sungyong Chang (Cornell University, Johnson Graduate School of Management); Fan Ye (UC Santa Barbara)
abstract: Across innovation-intensive industries, R&D progress often unfolds through discrete stages separated by transition periods with strategic implications for portfolio management and organizational performance, yet remain understudied. In pharmaceutical R&D, these transitions take the form of intervals between clinical trials – termed “whitespace” – which have received limited attention from a firm-level strategy and R&D management perspective. This exploratory analysis uses the Citeline TrialTrove database to examine 4,288 sequential clinical trial transitions (Phase I–II & Phase II–III) from industry-sponsored programs spanning 2008-2022. Whitespace is defined as the duration (in days) between the primary completion of one trial and the initiation of the subsequent trial. We quantify whitespace durations and assess heterogeneity and trends by trial phase, firm type (big vs. emerging pharmaceutical companies), molecule type (small molecule vs. biologics), and therapeutic area. Median whitespace duration was 474 days. Whitespace increased by 14.2% from 2008–2012 to 2018–2022, with notably greater increases in Phase I–II transitions (28.7%). Big pharmaceutical companies experienced greater increases (Phase I–II: 35.9%; Phase II–III: 17.2%) compared to emerging firms. Oncology and neurology experienced especially large increases. Longer whitespace was associated with lower drug subsequent development success. Taken together, these findings suggest that whitespace represents a substantial, growing, and heterogeneous component of drug development timelines. Whitespace may reflect strategic choices related to portfolio prioritization, risk management, capability deployment, and organizational coordination. Framing whitespace as an integral phase of R&D highlights opportunities for firms to better manage development transitions and improve innovation efficiency.

title: Preannounced Regulatory Inspections: FDA Oversight and Drug Quality Risk
authors: Zach Wright (Brigham Young University); John Gray (The Ohio State University Fisher College of Business); In Joon Noh (Korea University); George Ball (Indiana University Kelly School of Business)
abstract:
When inspecting a U.S. drug manufacturing facility, FDA inspectors arrive unannounced. However, in foreign countries
such as India, FDA inspectors provide significant advanced notice of their inspection, often many weeks or even months
before arriving. We examine the impact of these differing FDA inspection approaches on inspection outcomes and drug
quality. We first use 15 years of data from unannounced U.S. and preannounced Indian FDA inspections at over 200
facilities. Using a matching analysis to mimic the FDA’s model for selecting facilities for inspection, the 15-year dataset
indicates no significant difference in the odds of unannounced U.S. and preannounced Indian facilities receiving the most
severe inspection outcome, implying relatively equivalent drug manufacturing quality. Next, we examine previously unexplored data from two unannounced inspection pilots conducted by the FDA in India. These pilots enable us to disentangle
whether the equivalent inspection outcome result is indicative of similar drug quality or a greater difficulty of detecting
drug quality issues with preannounced inspections. We find that the odds of a facility receiving the most severe inspection
outcome are over 250% higher for unannounced inspections compared to preannounced inspections at the same facility in
India. Finally, using a matched sample of facilities producing over 3,000 drugs, we demonstrate potential consequences of
preannouncing inspections in India, showing that the number of serious adverse events for drugs made in Indian facilities
that experience preannounced inspections are significantly greater than for drugs made in matched facilities in the U.S.
that experience unannounced inspections. Our findings provide the first quantitative empirical evidence that preannouncing FDA inspections may allow drug manufacturers to operate with greater and undetected quality risk.

title: ‘Save the Life of My Child’: De-Risking Innovation and the Case of CAR T-Cell Therapy
authors: Kevin Chandra (Boston University)
abstract: Under what conditions do organizations and firms invest in a high-risk innovation, and how do changes in the non-market environment related to the innovation influence their investment decisions? A major consideration for organizations has been not only about technical feasibility and cost-benefit assessment, but also societal perception with regard to its potential benefits and risks. When an innovation is unproven, organizations, contingent on their resource availability, may either scale back their engagement or push through its development in spite of its risks. At present, however, the literature is split on organizational decisions on high-risk innovation, with some studies showing that firms push ahead when doing so maximizes their potential returns, whereas others demonstrate their tendency to ‘play safe’ due to high-risk perception. I seek to address this puzzle by focusing on CAR T-cell therapy, and specifically examining the case of Emily Whitehead, the world’s first child patient subjected to the then-experimental treatment in 2012 to treat leukemia. Using a difference-in-difference (DID) analysis by comparing CAR T-cell to other cell therapies not subject to ‘Emily shock’ throughout the 2000-2024 period, I found that after Emily’s successful treatment, there is a sharp and significant increase in the number of USPTO patent filings and clinical trials on CAR T-cell therapy relative to other cell therapy controls. Interestingly, for this cell therapy, I also observe a large increase in the amount of inter-firm collaboration and number of clinical trials on child patients with firms as lead sponsors. At the firm level, I also identify, on average, a gradual reallocation of resources from other types of cell therapy to CAR T-cell, highlighting a growing acceptance of this therapy, as well as the risk appetite among firms, to enter the technology. Nevertheless, additional heterogeneity analyses demonstrate that the effects are primarily driven by biotechnology firms, whereas the reallocation is more limited among major pharmaceutical companies.

title: Assessing the Security and Quality of the U.S. Military Health System Pharmaceutical Supply Chain: A Pilot Study (PhaSQ)
authors: Miranda Janvrin (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); Amandari Kanagartnam (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); Kyle Patrick Apilado (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); David Light (Valisure, LLC); Vic Suarez (Bluezonebio); Irwin Lucki (Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences); Tracey Koehlmoos (Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences)
abstract:
Abstract: The Nation and military readiness are impacted by the quality, safety, and availability of pharmaceutical products. The Assessing the Security and Quality of the U.S. Military Health System Pharmaceutical Supply Chain (PhaSQ) pilot study benefits the entire Nation by identifying and potentially mitigating the negative impacts of ineffective, impure, or unavailable pharmaceuticals. A lack of resilience and lack of transparency regarding quality in the supply chain, and the reliance on other countries to manufacture crucial drugs, are known national security risks. This project will be completed via four lines of effort. The first line of effort compares the essential medicines lists between the US Department of War (DoW), Food and Drug Administration, Department of Health and Human Services, and World Health Organization. The second line of effort synthesizes recommendations made to the DoW by other government agencies to strengthen its pharmaceutical supply chain. The third line of effort assesses the acceptability of a proposed “red, yellow, green” scoring tool for drug quality, which will include participants from the DoW, other federal agencies, and members from the private sector of the US healthcare system. The last line of effort, undertaken in partnership with Valisure, LLC, evaluates 42 drug products for quality and safety. To date we have completed the first two of our four lines of effort. All lines of effort are expected to be completed in 2026. Findings from this study are anticipated to inform decision making regarding sourcing and distribution of high-quality essential drug products.

title: Assessing the Acceptability of a Proposed Generic Pharmaceutical Quality Scoring Tool for Application in the United States and Military Health Systems
authors: Miranda Janvrin (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); Amandari Kanagaratnam (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); Kyle Patrick Apilado (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); Vivitha Mani (The Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine, Inc.); Tracey Koehlmoos (Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences)
abstract:
Abstract:
Introduction: The Department of War (DoW) commissioned a study to assess the quality and safety of pharmaceutical products critical to the operational needs of the Military Health System (MHS) and develop, apply, and test a quality scoring tool. In this study we aim to assess the acceptability, validity, and utility of a proposed quality scoring tool that incorporates various chemical analysis data.

Materials and Methods: The current study is a qualitative key informant interview study to assess the acceptability of the proposed scoring tool. We recruited participants who are key stakeholders involved in the DoW or US pharmaceutical supply chain, using purposive and snowball sampling. We provide participants with contextual information about the tool in advance of the virtual interview. Two interviewers are present for each interview; one leads the discussion with a pilot-tested interview guide, and the other interviewers record detailed notes. Thematic  analysis of responses will be conducted using NVivo.

Results: At present, we have conducted 16 out of an expected 30 interviews. Participants have provided insights into aspects of the proposed tool and the potential applicability of the tool within the DoW and US health system. We anticipate results from this study will inform policy making regarding sourcing and distribution of high-quality drug products for both the MHS and the Nation.

Conclusions: This is the first study to evaluate the acceptability of a generic pharmaceutical quality tool. We anticipate to complete all analysis and interpretation of results by May 2026.

title: Life cycle assessment of risk‑stratified breast cancer screening: a pathway‑based systems analysis
authors: Weijie Pan (Dartmouth College); Cassandra Thiel (New York University); Geoffrey Parker (Dartmouth College); Elizabeth Murnane (Dartmouth College); Katie Lichter (Dartmouth College)
abstract: The healthcare sector is a significant contributor to greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions, with radiology-intensive oncology services accounting for a substantial and growing share due to high energy demand, resource-intensive equipment, and medical-waste generation. Among oncology services, breast cancer screening and diagnostic care represents one of the most radiology-dependent clinical pathways in routine healthcare, yet the environmental impacts of this coordinated sequence of services have not been comprehensively assessed from a life-cycle perspective. Existing life-cycle assessments (LCAs) of breast cancer screening have largely focused on individual imaging modalities or isolated procedures, failing to capture the conditional, sequential, and organizational nature of real-world screening–diagnostic workflows and their dependence on patient-specific risk stratification decisions. In this study, we conduct a pathway-based life-cycle assessment of hypothetical risk-stratified pathways informed by current research for breast cancer screening and diagnostic care. The sequence of screening, recall, diagnostic imaging, biopsy, and pathology procedures is modelled for patients stratified into clinically defined low-, average-, elevated-, and high-risk groups, each associated with different expected volumes and intensities of imaging and diagnostic procedures. The results show that risk-stratified screening pathways are associated with an approximately 30% reduction in GHG emissions compared with conventional population-based screening models. Emissions are primarily driven by routine screening and downstream diagnostic procedures, highlighting the environmental benefits of risk-based screening strategies. Methodologically, this study advances healthcare LCA by shifting the analytical focus from individual technologies to entire clinical care pathways, and demonstrates how integrating clinically defined risk stratification can reorganize service delivery to reduce environmental impacts while maintaining clinical validity.

title: Type 2 Diabetes Screening under Capacity Constraints: A Health Care Systems Analysis
authors: Ruopeng An (New York University); Zhixin Cao (University of Chicago); Zezheng Lin (University of Chicago); Fengqi Zhang (National University of Singapore); Yuhao Wang (University of Chicago)
abstract:
In the United States, type 2 diabetes and prediabetes affect a large and growing share of the adult population, yet a substantial proportion of high-risk individuals remain undiagnosed. In practice, diabetes screening operates not merely as a clinical decision, but as an institutionalized gatekeeping mechanism shaped by clinical guidelines, payment incentives, and care delivery workflows. BMI-based thresholds have become the dominant criterion for determining screening eligibility, embedding a simple and scalable rule into routine practice. However, in a post-pandemic environment characterized by persistent primary care workforce shortages, constrained screening capacity, and increasing heterogeneity in population risk profiles, reliance on legacy screening rules raises important system-level and policy questions.

When screening criteria are institutionalized as gateways to preventive care, their design influences not only clinical efficiency but also the perceived fairness and social legitimacy of health care systems. Persistent misalignment between formal screening thresholds and underlying risk distributions may allow unmet health needs to accumulate outside the system, potentially generating sustained policy pressure on medical and insurance institutions. These concerns are particularly salient for individuals who do not meet conventional obesity criteria but nonetheless face elevated metabolic risk, highlighting the need to reassess how screening opportunities are prioritized under resource constraints.

This study conceptualizes type 2 diabetes screening as a capacity-constrained health care system decision problem rather than solely a predictive task. Using nationally representative survey data from the United States, the analysis compares traditional BMI-based screening rules with an alternative risk-based prioritization approach derived from explainable risk stratification models using non-laboratory variables. Methodologically, the study applies explainable risk-based models to evaluate the system-level performance and missed-case distributions of alternative screening rules under fixed screening capacity constraints. By holding the overall proportion of individuals screened constant, the analysis mirrors real-world limitations faced by health systems and payers, allowing a direct comparison of how different rules allocate limited screening resources across populations.

The study focuses on detection efficiency, patterns of under-detection, and subgroup differences, with particular attention to normal-weight adults and demographic heterogeneity. Rather than presupposing superiority of any single approach, the analysis evaluates whether risk-ranked screening strategies offer potential advantages in aligning screening decisions with population risk under uncertainty.

Overall, this study aims to provide a policy-relevant analytical framework and empirical evidence base to support reassessment and potential updating of U.S. type 2 diabetes screening guidelines. More broadly, it illustrates how screening rule design functions as a system-level policy choice with implications for efficiency, equity, and institutional credibility in capacity-constrained health care systems.

title: Reformulation and Algorithmic Framework for Fractional Queueing-Based Optimization Problems
authors: Nguyen Nam (George Washington University); Miguel Lejeune (George Washington University)
abstract:
We develop a comprehensive framework for modeling, reformulating, and solving network design queueing-based optimization problems. The network consists of a series of interdependent queueing systems with variable number of servers and endogenous service time and arrival rate, and aims at responding promptly to time-sensitive demand. Defining the number of servers deployed at a facility as a decision variable significantly increases the complexity of the problem formulation. The resulting model is a fractional nonlinear integer problem that includes factorial, polynomial, and exponential terms, as well as summations where the term count is a decision variable. The MILP reformulation framework encompasses five main steps and is general enough to be applied to the main queueing systems, such as M/M/K, M/G/K, G/M/K, and G/G/K. Specifically, we introduce new quasi-multilinearization and multilinearization processes for high-degree polynomials and develop novel analytical methods providing closed-form formulae to calculate the coefficients of multilinear monomials. We devise a branch-and-cut algorithm, solving at each node. an outer approximation of the MILP problem which is gradually tightened through the dynamic introduction of lazy constraints and valid inequalities. 
Notably, we derive a new family of nested valid inequalities and demonstrate their computational effectiveness.  To test our approach, we consider the problem of designing a responsive network for medical emergencies (cardiac arrests, opioid overdoes). The objective is to minimize the average response time to urgent demands and to increase the chance of survival of patients, while deciding the location of facilities, and the deployment and assignment of emergency vehicles. Numerical tests on real data show the applicability of the reformulation and algorithmic framework.

title: Stochastic Pandemic Mitigation Model: Ensuring ICU Access Without Overburdening Society
authors: Janne Kettunen (The George Washington University); Miguel Lejeune (The George Washington University)
abstract: Key objectives for policymakers deciding on pandemic mitigation include safeguarding the healthcare system by ensuring reliable access to ICUs for patients, while simultaneously limiting mitigation measures to avoid overburdening society. These goals are pursued under uncertainty in the illness's transmission rate. We propose a multi-period mixed-integer nonlinear chance-constrained stochastic programming framework that addresses these requirements. We capture the pandemic dynamics through a compartmental epidemic model. We design a solution method that features the (i) deterministic and equivalent reformulation of the nonlinear chance constraint using a Boolean method, (ii) quadratization of the set of nonconvex constraints via linearization techniques for polynomial terms and exponential functions with integer arguments, (iii) construction of the envelope of bilinear terms defined on a specific domain with a non-trivial upper bound on the product of two variables, and (iv) derivation of valid inequalities exploiting the problem's combinatorial structure. The proposed framework generalizes well to alternative mitigation functions and is applicable to nonconvex polynomial chance-constrained problems beyond epidemic mitigation. Our experiments with COVID-19 data confirm the computational efficiency and scalability of our approach, demonstrating that the solutions are stable, reliable and perform well out-of-sample, and robust even under uncertainties in other key model parameters. Our results show that it may be optimal to delay the onset of mitigation and that the optimal strategy can include periods of lenient mitigation in between. This research addresses a gap in the literature on nonconvex polynomial chance-constrained problems and introduces a new second-order cone formulation for the envelope of bilinear terms.

title: Hospital Stockpiling Ahead of Shortages: Evidence from the US Opioid Supply Chain
authors: Hanu Tyagi (University of Illinois Urbana Champaign); Iman Attari (University of Cincinnati)
abstract: Drug shortages in the United States remain persistent. When shortages occur, timely and equitable access to the affected drugs and clinical substitutes is essential for patient care. Yet we know little about which hospitals secure supply ahead of and during an imminent shortage. We examine the 2017 nationwide, supply-induced shortage of injectable opioids using multi-echelon transaction data, and ask: (1) how the remaining inventory is distributed once production is disrupted, and (2) how substitutes are accessed in the period surrounding the event. We find uneven allocation and substantial pre-shortage stockpiling of substitutes by a small subset of hospitals, reinforcing “haves vs. have-nots” disparities in pharmaceutical access.

title: Appointment Reliability in Primary Care: Evidence from Adults With ADHD in Epic Scheduling Data
authors: Christopher Kwaramba (Virginia Commonwealth University); Jeffrey Shockley (Virginia Commonwealth University); Shannon Harris (Virginia Commonwealth University); Jeffrey Smith (Virginia Commonwealth University); Kishu Chaudry (Virginia Tech School of Medicine)
abstract: Missed outpatient primary care appointments reduce access and disrupt clinic schedules, yet the drivers of cancellations and no shows remain incompletely understood in large health systems. This study examines whether adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibit different appointment completion patterns than adults without ADHD in internal medicine and family medicine clinics and quantifies the implications for appointment reliability. Using Epic scheduling data, we construct an appointment level panel including all scheduled primary care appointments during calendar year 2024, regardless of final status (completed, canceled, or no show). ADHD status is defined at the patient level using diagnosis history recorded anywhere in the health system, reducing misclassification that can occur when ADHD is identified only from visit level coding. The primary outcomes are cancellation probability, no show probability, and timing of cancellations relative to the scheduled appointment time. Secondary outcomes include rescheduling frequency and time to next completed primary care visit following a missed appointment. We estimate adjusted differences between ADHD and non ADHD patients using regression models with clinic and provider fixed effects and controls for demographics, payer class, and comorbidity indicators. To strengthen causal interpretation, we exploit within clinic variation over time and conduct sensitivity analyses using alternative ADHD definitions, including problem list based identification and medication evidence. The study contributes to operations management research by providing a scalable measurement approach for appointment reliability using electronic health record scheduling traces and by clarifying whether a clinically identifiable patient segment is associated with systematically different patterns of cancellations and no shows. Findings can inform targeted scheduling and outreach strategies aimed at improving access and continuity in primary care.

title: Strategic Reserves: Shelved Innovation as a Real Option
authors: Elisabeth Hofmeister (Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition)
abstract: How can firms mitigate risk in research and development? This paper investigates the role of shelved innovation - R&D projects suspended despite promising results - as a risk management tool in the pharmaceutical industry. I identify ‘shelved’ drug development projects, those suspended following positive trial results, using a novel dataset linking clinical trials to their disclosed results. Conceptually, shelved innovation represents a real option to the firm that can be strategically created and exercised. First, I investigate option creation and demonstrate that firms create shelved R&D projects through simultaneously investing in multiple competing projects. Second, I examine the conditions under which firms choose to exercise the option and restart a project. Using the exogenous nature of trial failures, I evaluate whether firms restart shelved projects following project failures in the same market. Results show that firms restart shelved projects in response to late-stage failures in Phase III clinical trials.  Further, I find that the decision to restart a shelved project is moderated by the presence of co-specialized complementary assets and the thickness of the market for technology, an alternative source of replacements for failed R&D projects. Lastly, I provide evidence on the performance implications of restarting shelved projects and find no signal of inferior performance, both in terms of transition and relabeling probabilities. These findings support the view that shelved innovation is not an arbitrary byproduct of the R&D process, but represents a real option to the firm that is employed to manage risk.

title: Turning a Blind Eye: Role of Pharmacy–Supplier Sourcing Channels in the Opioid Epidemic
authors: Iman Attari (University of Cincinnati); Robert Wiedmer (Arizona State University); Jorge Mejia (Indiana University Bloomington); Jonathan Helm (Indiana University Bloomington)
abstract: With more than 645,000 deaths since the 1990s, the opioid crisis has been one of the worst health crises in the United States. Previous research has demonstrated that the crisis is primarily initiated and fueled by the oversupply of prescription opioids. This trend has raised significant concerns regarding the effectiveness of government monitoring efforts, which rely on pharmaceutical suppliers to identify and report suspicious pharmacy orders. In response, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has primarily blamed large national suppliers and increased regulatory pressure on them. In contrast to the DEA's focus on large suppliers, we investigate how pharmacies' use of other sourcing channels contributes to over-dispensing. Using the DEA's ARCOS database and leveraging the 2010 OxyContin reformulation as a quasi-experiment, we analyze more than 350 million opioid transactions between 610 suppliers and 90,920 pharmacies in the US from 2006 to 2014. Our results show that independent pharmacies sourcing a higher share of opioids from small suppliers and chain pharmacies engaging in the self-distribution of drugs through their vertically-integrated supply network exhibit higher levels of over-dispensing. Specifically, independent pharmacies with a 10 percentage point higher share of small suppliers and chain pharmacies with a 10 percentage point higher share of self-distribution in their supply base exhibit 2.6% and 7.2% higher over-dispensing, respectively. We further provide evidence on how the sourcing strategies of pharmacies are associated with higher prescription opioid-related mortality rates at the county level. These findings suggest that focusing regulatory efforts on large national suppliers may overlook the role of supply network characteristics contributing to drug diversion. By highlighting the roles of small suppliers and self-distribution practices, our study underscores the need for a more comprehensive regulatory approach to combat the opioid epidemic effectively.

title: Regulating Powerful Intermediaries: The Impact of Curbing Intermediary Practices on Supply Chain Outcomes
authors: Nikhil Sharma (Ohio State University - Fisher College of Business); John Gray (Ohio State University); Jurriaan De Jong (Ohio State University - Fisher College of Business)
abstract:
Supply Chain Intermediaries (SCIs) account for a significant share of economic activity across many product industries, contributing over one-third of the United States’ gross domestic product (GDP). We observe an increasingly common pattern in which SCIs have gained considerable power, such as traders in agriculture, distributors in alcohol, or GPOs in the healthcare industry, and have adopted practices to extract disproportionate gains in the supply chain. In this paper, we examine how regulating such practices of powerful SCIs affects supply chain outcomes. We focus on retail pharmacy as our context and Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) as SCIs that not only manage pharmacy claims but also, as powerful SCIs, determine which drugs will be covered and how much retailers and manufacturers will be paid, thereby influencing the flow of products, money, and information across the supply chain.
We focus on regulating the ‘Spread Pricing’ practice in which the SCI charges payers (government entities or private employers who pay for products purchased by eligible members or employees as part of a benefit plan) more than it reimburses retailers (from whom the members or employees buy the products) and retains the difference, known as ‘spread,’ an amount determined by and proprietary to the SCI. In our context, Spread Pricing was among the first SCI practices to attract scrutiny, including a payer audit in the Ohio Medicaid program that found a $208M (31.4%) spread charged by SCIs in 2018, which led the payer to ban this practice beginning in 2019. We leverage this exogenous event to investigate whether implementing the ban improved SCI practices and supply chain outcomes. We use secondary data from CMS Medicaid across multiple US states and employ the Synthetic Control Method with Forward Selection Panel Data Approach (fsPDA) to construct a synthetic control unit, Synthetic Ohio, as a weighted average of control states that resemble Ohio but did not experience the policy intervention.
By comparing Ohio with Synthetic Ohio, we found an initial and significant decline in payer expenditures between Q2 2018 (when the audit was conducted) and Q1 2019 (when the ban was enforced). However, we found an overall increase of approximately 15% in payer expenditures post-ban. We further applied a difference-in-differences approach and found that, compared with neighboring states, Ohio's post-ban drug sourcing shifted toward manufacturing facilities outside the United States, which have been associated with lower quality standards. To summarize, the ban on Spread Pricing in Ohio led to an overall increase in payer expenditures and a counterintuitive shift in drug sourcing toward lower-quality drugs. 
Our study has practical implications for regulators and other supply chain members regarding how banning SCI practices may elicit counterresponses from powerful SCIs, thereby contributing to ongoing policy debates in the retail pharmacy industry, particularly as other states consider adopting similar regulations to curb intermediary power. Our research also has broader implications for other industries—such as food, agriculture, alcohol, and healthcare—where powerful SCIs increasingly dominate and where similar regulatory challenges are emerging.

title: Offshore Manufacturing of Innovative Drugs: Evidence from U.S. Pharmaceutical Firms’ Reliance on Specialized Drug Manufacturers
authors: Minji Lee (Cornell University); Sungyong Chang (Cornell University)
abstract: Pharmaceutical manufacturing often separates drug development from large-scale production through contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs). Over the past two decades, United States pharmaceutical firms have increasingly relied on offshore CDMOs, drawing sustained attention from patients, regulators, and the media due to concerns over drug supply security. We argue that entrepreneurial pharmaceutical firms are more likely than established firms to rely on offshore CDMOs. Entrepreneurial firms typically lack the financial and manufacturing resources needed for in-house production. Although external partnerships can alleviate these constraints, collaborations with established firms expose entrepreneurial firms to heightened risks of knowledge appropriation. Consequently, entrepreneurial firms turn to specialized third-party manufacturers, particularly CDMOs. Because manufacturing experience for pharmaceutical products is unevenly distributed across locations, with a substantial share accumulated by CDMOs located outside the U.S., this reliance often takes the form of offshore contracting rather than partnerships with domestic manufacturers. This reliance intensifies when entrepreneurial firms develop first-mover products. We define first-mover products as first-in-class drugs that introduce a new mechanism of action, thereby giving rise to a new therapeutic class. Developing such drugs requires scaling production processes under heightened regulatory scrutiny and limited prior manufacturing precedent, further increasing reliance on offshore CDMOs. Using a 2025 cross-sectional sample of U.S. pharmaceutical manufacturing contracts, we find results consistent with our arguments. These findings suggest that pharmaceuticals particularly important for patients—those developed by entrepreneurial firms and involving first-in-class drugs—are disproportionately manufactured offshore, revealing a source of vulnerability in the U.S. pharmaceutical supply chain.

title: Response Latency in Asynchronous Care Queues and ED Utilization: LLM-Based Measurement of Patient Message Acuity and Complexity
authors: Mohamed Megahed, Nathan Craig, Jane Jiang, Aravind Chandrasekaran
abstract: Operational delays in decentralized service systems can induce cross-channel substitutions. Digital patient portals provide a novel setting in which delayed response may shift demand toward the emergency department (ED). Studying this mechanism is difficult because structured records do not capture the severity and complexity embedded in patient messages at arrival. We address this measurement problem with an LLM-based pipeline that scores patient-initiated medical advice messages, then combine these text-derived measures with a discrete-time hazard model of downstream ED utilization. Results from 441,806 patient-initiated threads suggest that unanswered messages predict higher short-run ED use, concentrated early in the waiting period. The study shows how AI can recover latent demand signals from unstructured patient text and suggests that some ED demand reflects operational delays among patients who already have outpatient access, not only uninsured access gaps.

title: The Foreign Inspection Gap: FDA GMP Oversight of U.S. Drug Imports, 2014–2024
authors: George Kwiecinski (Global Key Solutions)
abstract: From 2014 to 2024, U.S. drug imports rose sharply while FDA foreign GMP inspections fell. Analyzing FDA inspection records against import volumes, we found that for every additional billion dollars of drug imports between 2014 and 2019, 23 fewer inspections occurred. Inspection intensity in China dropped from 101.8 to 18.3 inspections per billion USD over the decade. Foreign facility outcome rates with observations ran 1.3 to 1.8 times higher than the U.S. baseline of 49.3 percent, with China at 69.0 percent and India at 62.3 percent. Disparities between MRA and non-MRA countries persisted across the period. These findings provide empirical support for the FDA's May 6, 2025, shift to unannounced foreign inspections and highlight the need for oversight metrics that scale with the globalization of pharmaceutical manufacturing.
